verses.note: Later Scripture pictures a river flowing from God's dwelling to give life: from the temple in Ezekiel 47, from the city of God in Psalm 46:4, and from the throne of God and the Lamb in Revelation 22:1. That pattern is one of the clues many readers follow in seeing Eden as the first sanctuary, the place where God's presence is the source of life.

The verb for God's walking is the language of his presence in Israel's sanctuary (Leviticus 26:11-12). Eden is where God and humanity met, and the tragedy of this verse is that the people flee the very presence they were made for.

The guarded eastern entrance and the cherubim make Eden the pattern for the tabernacle, where access to God's presence was barred by a curtain woven with cherubim. The New Testament says that way was opened by Christ's death (Hebrews 10:19-20), and the last chapter of the Bible reopens the tree of life (Revelation 22:2).

If Moriah is the temple mount, as 2 Chronicles 3:1 indicates, the place where God provided a substitute for Isaac became the place where Israel's sacrifices were offered for centuries. The verse gives the temple its first meaning: the place where God provides and appears.

Jacob's words give Israel's later worship its basic vocabulary: a place where God chooses to meet people is his house, and it is a gate between heaven and earth. The tabernacle and temple carry that idea, and John presents Jesus himself as the place where heaven is opened (John 1:51, 2:19-21).
The family that will serve at God's dwelling first appears as three boys going down to Egypt. Israel's worship grows out of a family's history, not out of an institution founded from nothing.
A list of names in Egypt looks forward to the service of God's dwelling in the wilderness. Before the tabernacle is built, the families who will carry and guard it are already named.

The inner room is the place where God's presence is focused on earth, above the ark. The verse makes the tabernacle a real meeting place between God and Israel, dangerous because real, and it explains why the way into that room is so carefully controlled.

God's dwelling is among an impure people, and their sin does not leave it untouched. The verse holds together the wonder that God lives among sinners and the cost of that nearness: his house must be cleansed of what they bring into it.

God's presence with Israel was never tied to a building. The tabernacle traveled with the people; the later temple is a gift God allows, not a need he has. Stephen makes the same point in Acts 7:44-50.

The temple is built for God's name, the revelation of who he is, rather than as a house God needs. Solomon's dedication prayer states the point when it says that heaven cannot contain God, much less a house (1 Kings 8:27).
The climax of restoration is not the land or the king but God's sanctuary among his people. The book will end with the city's new name, ‘The LORD Is There’ (48:35).

The tabernacle word announces that God's presence will again be among his people as it was in the wilderness, now forever. The New Testament uses the same tent language for the incarnation, the church, and the new creation.

The sanctuary is ‘Your sanctuary’: its ruin is a dishonor to God before it is a loss to Israel. Chapter 9 moves from this prayer for a desolate temple to a prophecy in which the temple's fate is bound up with the coming of an anointed one.

The temple, God's appointed place of meeting with Israel, will be destroyed. Mark has just shown Jesus judging it (11:15-17) and will soon report the claim that he would build another not made with hands (14:58). The Gospel points to Jesus himself as the new center of God's presence.
Desecration of the temple signals the end of that temple's role. The chapter's movement from admiring the stones (verse 1) to fleeing the city (verse 14) shows the old center of worship giving way.

The disciples return to the temple, not away from it. Luke's story of the church begins inside Israel's worship, and Acts keeps the apostles in the temple courts (Acts 2:46, 3:1) until the gospel moves out from Jerusalem to the nations.

God's dwelling with Israel in the tabernacle and temple now takes a human form. John will later have Jesus speak of his body as the temple (2:19-21), and Revelation 21:3 uses the same verb for God's final dwelling with his people.
Jacob called the place of his dream Bethel, the house of God and the gate of heaven. Jesus places that meeting point in himself, preparing for his later claim that his body is the temple (2:21).

The language of filling recalls God's glory filling the tabernacle and temple (Exodus 40:34, 1 Kings 8:11). The church, filled with Christ, is the dwelling of God that 2:21-22 will call a holy temple in the Lord.

The temple, the place where God's presence dwelt in Israel, becomes a people. The Gentiles who were shut out by the temple's barrier are now built into the sanctuary itself. The same idea appears in 1 Corinthians 3:16 and 1 Peter 2:5.
The Septuagint wording of Psalm 68:16 makes Christ the new place of God's dwelling, as Zion and its temple were. John 1:14 and 2:21 make the same move with different images.
